entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lewis of Luxembourg (c. 1391 – September 27, 1443), a scion of the powerful House of Luxembourg and a prominent ecclesiastical statesman, served as a key figure bridging Anglo-French political and religious spheres during the latter half of the Hundred Years' War. His career, marked by rapid ascent through the church hierarchy — from Bishop of Thérouanne to Archbishop of Rouen, then Bishop of Ely, and finally Cardinal — underscored the intricate web of diplomacy, loyalty, and ambition that characterized the Lancastrian occupation of France and the early reign of Henry VI. As a trusted counselor to the English regency government in France and later in England, he wielded considerable influence in both temporal and spiritual affairs, particularly in the administration of English territories in France.

Born around 1391, Lewis of Luxembourg began his ecclesiastical career in a Europe deeply fractured by the Western Schism and the ongoing conflict between England and France. Appointed Bishop of Thérouanne in 1415, he quickly aligned himself with the Anglo-Burgundian cause, becoming a staunch supporter of the English administration in occupied France. Following the death of John of Lancaster, Duke of Bedford, in 1435, Lewis was elevated to Archbishop of Rouen in 1436, a strategically vital see in English Normandy. His transfer to the wealthy English diocese of Ely in 1437 further solidified his position within the Lancastrian establishment. He achieved the cardinalate on December 18, 1439, a testament to his political utility and connections within the Curia, though his brief tenure as a cardinal saw him primarily engaged in English domestic and foreign policy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lewis of Luxembourg was a pivotal figure in Anglo-French relations during the Hundred Years' War, serving as a key ecclesiastical administrator and diplomat who helped sustain English power in France. His career demonstrates the intricate fusion of church and state power in late medieval Europe, impacting the administrative and diplomatic strategies of the Lancastrian dual monarchy.
